lesson.title: Put a proportionate quality system in place
lesson.summary: Build a written quality system with proportionate implementation and preserved rigour.

prerequisites.reason: Risk management is one of its processes.
The provider must implement the system

blocks: A **quality-management system** uses systematic written policies, procedures and instructions to ensure compliance. It includes a compliance strategy and change management, design/control/verification, development/quality assurance, and test/validation procedures with frequencies.
Name accountable people and how decisions produce records. A folder of policy titles without operating procedures does not establish implementation.

It also covers technical specifications and standards or alternative compliance means, data operations, risk management, post-market monitoring, serious-incident reporting and communications with authorities, assessment bodies, operators and customers.

Post-market monitoring gathers evidence after supply; serious-incident reporting has a specific statutory route. Detailed Articles 72–73 procedures are later-course work, but a quality system must include them rather than waiting for an incident.

Include relevant documentation/record procedures, resources and security of supply, and management/staff accountability. **Proportionate implementation** fits the organisation’s size, particularly SMEs, start-ups and SMCs.

SMEs and SMCs are defined enterprise size categories; verify eligibility under the applicable definitions. Proportionate processes still preserve the required rigour and level of protection. Small size is not a waiver of risk management or accountability.

**Sector integration** allows the required aspects within an equivalent sector-law quality function. Specified financial institutions’ Union financial-law governance can fulfil much of the quality-system obligation.

The financial equivalence excludes Article 17(1)(g), (h), (i): risk management, post-market monitoring and serious-incident reporting. Preserve these aspects. Also take the relevant harmonised standards into account; do not assume a standard’s current publication status.

Case: a small Northbridge team proposes informal chat approval with no owner for incident reporting or record keeping. A simpler documented process can be proportionate, but the missing responsibilities still need to be supplied.

Evidence should show who acts, when, using what criteria, how records are retained and how the procedure is reviewed. This is a practical way to inspect the statutory system, not a mandatory template.
